abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Dyslipidemic statins reduce blood and brain cholinesterase (ChE) activities in mice, with scarce information on other protein/enzyme targets. The study aims at conducting a mini meta-analysis on in vivo and in vitro adverse anti-ChE effects of atorvastatin, simvastatin and rosuvastatin in mice, and using the SwissPrediction to identify in silico body target proteins. The data comprised 72 records of plasma, erythrocytes and brain ChE activities, expressed as percent mean ± SD of respective controls. We conducted a randomized effects size single-arm meta-analysis. The risk of bias scoring was according to those of animal experiments. The effect size (% ChE activity) of statin treatments was significantly decreased by 25.85 % (combined effect size=74.15, p = 0.0001), with significant heterogeneity (Q=1133.19, p < 0.0001, I2=93.73 %). Subgroup analysis was significantly dose and concentration-dependent. The funnel plot showed non-symmetrical data distribution, with no imputed points. The risk of bias was moderate. In silico mouse body protein targets for the statins were mainly classes of Family AG protein- coupled receptor (20.0 %-33.3 %), Oxidoreductase (6.7–13.3 %) and Eraser (13.3 % each), with others at 0–26.7 %. The findings highlight statin effects in mice by reducing blood and brain ChE activities, in a dose/concentration-dependent manner, that would potentially modulate the cholinergic system. This anti-ChE effect together with in silico protein targets recognized could be the basis of further experimental explorations of adverse effects of statins.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Dyslipidemic statins such as simvastatin, pravastatin, atorvastatin, rosuvastatin fluvastatin and pitavastatin are widely used clinically to decrease serum cholesterol levels by inhibiting 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A, which is the rate-limiting target enzymatic metabolic step in the liver [1], [2]. Despite the similarity in the clinical outcome of statins by reducing blood cholesterol, low-density lipoproteins and triglyceride levels, they vary considerably in their pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics profiles [3], [4]. Statins are also characterized by having pleiotropic effects [5].

Adverse actions of statins mainly involve the liver and skeletal muscles [6], [7] paralleled with central nervous system (CNS) effects [8], [9]. As statin intolerance was reported clinically [10], [11], several experimental animal studies highlighted the adverse effects of statins in an attempt to produce an animal model of statin intolerance [9], [12], [13], [14], [15], [16], [17], [18], [19]. Modulatory effects of statins on several body systems with potential additional pleiotropic actions and intolerance characteristics have been reported in experimental animals. These include neurobehavioral and cognitive functional changes and metabolomic alterations (profiles of metabolites) in biological fluids, the blood and several organ systems in laboratory animals such as rats, mice and young chicks [9], [12], [13], [14], [15], [16], [17], [18], [19], [20]. Examples of metabolomic changes produced by statins include but are not limited to reduced blood and brain cholinesterase (ChE) activities, oxidative stress by increasing blood and tissue malondialdehyde (MDA) levels and reducing glutathione content, changes in liver enzymes activities indicating liver injury, circulating proteoglycan endocan as well as changes in amino acids levels [15], [16], [17], [18], [19], [20], [21], [22].

Recently, we have attempted to describe the undesirable/adverse effects of three statins (atorvastatin, simvastatin and rosuvastatin) following experimental single or repeated doses in mice [14], [15], [16], [17]. These effects were characterized by neurobehavioral alterations that included exploratory open-field depression, negative geotaxis performance, head pocking behavior, forced swimming endurance and altered responses to anesthesia or intoxication [14], [16], [17]. In parallel with these effects specific biochemical alterations reported in statin-treated mice included inhibition of blood and brain ChE activities, increased MDA level, decreased GSH level, and increased liver enzymes [14], [15], [16], [17]. However, the precise mechanisms of action of statins in inducing adverse effects described above and those in the literature are not yet clear. Nevertheless, they might targeting specific proteins such as the ChE, cellular membranes, or tissue redox oxidant/antioxidant systems [12], [13], [14], [15], [16], [17], [18], [23], [24]. Hence, the current study presents a mini meta-analysis [25] of the overall in vivo and in vitro adverse anti-ChE effects of statins (atorvastatin, simvastatin and rosuvastatin), comprising 72 records, we reported recently in mice [14], [16], [17], [26], as well as using the SwissPrediction webserver [27], [28] to identify in silico body target proteins of the three statins in mice for possible future exploratory studies, since such information is not available in the literature.

sec.title: Ethical approval
sec.p: The present study and those used for the mini meta-analysis [14], [15], [16], [17], [26] were approved by the Scientific Committee on Research and Animal Care and Use and the Committee of Postgraduate Studies at the College of Veterinary Medicine, University of Mosul, Iraq, as well as by the Institutional Review Board of the College of Veterinary Medicine, University of Mosul (No. 2144, November 2, 2022) and the University of Mosul (No. 4S/29927, October 30, 2022) to study statins in mice as an experimental animal model. The use of mice experimentally in the studies included in the present meta-analysis [14], [16], [17], [26] was according to institutional regulations and ethics which were derived from guidelines of Animal Research: Reporting of In Vivo Experiments (ARRIVE) (https://www.nc3rs.org.uk/arrive-guidelines) and the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals [29]. The study did not include humans or their tissues.

sec.p: The study project was registered at AsPredicted (https://aspredicted.org/, No. 180620; June 24, 2024; https://aspredicted.org/yy5hi.pdf)

sec.title: Study period and location
sec.p: We conducted this study from January 2, 2024 to October 1, 2024, at the College of Veterinary Medicine, University of Mosul, Iraq.

sec.title: Data extraction
sec.p: The data of experimental anti-ChE effects of the three statins (atorvastatin, simvastatin and rosuvastatin) in male mice of Swiss origin were extracted from tables and figures of selected publications [14], [16], [17], [26], and they were tabulated as shown in Table 1. They comprised observational data (Total=483) of 72 records of plasma (n = 156), erythrocytes (n = 96) and brain (n = 231) ChE activities reported in mice following statins treatments in vivo or in vitro [14], [16], [17], [26]. Table 1 presents percentages (mean ± SD) of ChE activities relative to their respective control values. In this manner, the data can be subjected to randomized effects size one-arm meta-analysis [30] to answer the specific inquiry, of whether or not the three statins generally alter the ChE activity in mice. Mini meta-analysis can be applied to such data [25], [31] to examine the overall anti-ChE effects of the three statins as derived from our recent publications [14], [16], [17], [26]. Other studies were not considered for the present analysis, since they have used different experimental protocols, and/or animal species [9], [12], [13], [18], [19], [32].

sec.title: Meta-analysis and statistics
sec.p: For the meta-analysis, we used the software program Meta-Essentials, Version 1.5 (Erasmus Research Institute of Management, Rotterdam, Netherlands) [30]. Using this tool we conducted a randomized effects size single-arm meta-analysis, which included mainly the forest plot, publication bias, subgroup analysis as well as other related statistics [30], [33]. Subgroup analysis was conducted to analyze the effect size (depressed ChE activity) under different doses and concentrations of the three statins [30], [33]. The Cochrane Q-test (p < 0.10) and calculated I2 were used to assess the data heterogeneity [34], [35]. The funnel plot and Egger’s regression test were used to assess the publication bias [35], [36], [37].

sec.title: Risk of bias
sec.p: The possibility of the existence of risk of bias in the studies selected for the meta-analysis complied with the scoring system for bias detection in animal experiments [38], [39], [40]. The risk of bias depends on the evaluation of six items (selection: allocation, similarity and allocation; performance: housing randomization and intervention blindness; detection: selection randomization and blind evaluation; attrition; reporting, and other interfering problems) [38], [39], [40]. They were scored as “yes” (score of 2-low bias), “no” (score of 0-high bias) and “unclear” (score of 1-moderate bias). We used the online Risk of Bias Visualization (rovis) tool to evaluate the risk of bias [41]. Other than the specific statistical procedures mentioned above, the statistical software PAST 4.15 (https://www.nhm.uio.no/english/research/resources/past/) was used for descriptive statistical analysis of the data.

sec.title: Identification of the mouse protein targets for statins
sec.p: The chemical structural formulae representing the canonical Simplified Molecular-Input Line-Entry System (SMILE) of the three statins (atorvastatin, simvastatin and rosuvastatin) were obtained from PubChem (https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/). Each formula was separately fed to the SwissTargetPrediction web server (http://www.swisstargetprediction.ch/) to predict and identify potential protein targets in the mouse (Mus musculus) body. This online in silico tool identifies important protein targets of rats, mice and humans for certain molecular weight drugs, and recognizes potential sites of drug action, interaction, or toxicity which could be in association with the management of certain disease conditions [28], [42], [43]. We focused in the present attempt to identify protein targets on the highest percentages (> 6.7 %) predicted by the in silico Swiss TargetPrediction web server of the mouse body proteins as potential targets for the three statins, which were reported to cause ChE inhibition in vivo and in vitro [14], [16], [17], [26].

sec.title: Statins and ChE activity in mice
sec.p: The 72 ChE activity records in the plasma (n = 156), erythrocytes (n = 96) and brain (n = 231) of mice following in vivo treatments with, or in vitro exposure to the statins atorvastatin, simvastatin and rosuvastatin are shown in Table 1. The reductions in plasma, erythrocyte and brain ChE activities following in vivo treatments of mice with the three statins ranged as 25.8 %-53.4 %, 11.3 %-47.7 %, and 12.8–53.8 %, respectively, whereas those of the plasma and brain after in vitro exposure to statins were 0.3 %-41.4 % and 0.6 %-51.2 %, respectively, relative to respective control values (Table 1).

sec.title: Mini meta-analysis
sec.p: The single-arm randomized effects model meta-analysis of the 72 records, revealed a forest plot showing percentages of plasma, erythrocyte, or brain ChE activities among mice following in vivo or in vitro statin treatments relative to respective controls (Fig. 1). The standardized effect size (% ChE activity) of statin treatment groups when compared to controls was significantly decreased by 25.85 %. Other statistical outcomes associated with the forest plot were as follows: combined effect size= 74.15, SE= 1.73, 95 % C.I., lower and upper limits= 70.7 and 77.61, respectively, and Z value= 42.82 with two-tailed p-value= 0.0001 (Fig. 1). Relative weights of the 72 ChE activity records were close to each other and they ranged between 0.87 % and 1.59 % (Fig. 1).

caption.p: Forest plot of 72 study records (effect size as % of respective controls, and their comparative weightings) used for mini meta-analysis of plasma, erythrocyte and brain cholinesterase activities in experimental mice treated with statins.

sec.title: Analysis of heterogeneity analysis
sec.p: As depicted in Fig. 1, statistical analysis of heterogeneity revealed that% of ChE activities were remarkably heterogeneous. This was supported by the highly significant Cochrane Q-test (Q= 1133.19, p < 0.0001) and high heterogeneity indices (I2=93.73 %, T2=132.95, T = 11.53). Despite this heterogeneity, standardized residuals (based on Z-scores of an individual study record) were normally distributed around the combined effect size, the Galbraith regression analysis of Z score vs. inverse SE, revealed the location of effect size points within the lower and upper limits of the regression line, and the data points were not located below the no-effect zero (y = 0) line, whereas outliers of the data points were not detected by the normal quantile plot (Fig. 2).

caption.p: Plots of normal distribution, Galbraith regression and quantile distribution of plasma, erythrocyte and brain cholinesterase activities in experimental mice treated with statins.

sec.title: Subgroup analysis
sec.p: Because of the high data heterogeneity described above, subgroup analysis of the data with regards to statin doses/concentrations used showed a relatively high pseudo R2 value (78.4 %), and the associated forest plot of subgroup analysis revealed that reductions in ChE activity in mice were dose and concentration-dependent (Fig. 3, Table 2). The subgroup-related effect sizes, 95 % C.I., and their supportive statistics are shown in Table 2. Highly significant (PQ < 0.0001) effect sizes were seen with statin doses given at single (500 or 100 mg/kg) or at repeated doses (200 mg/kg/day) for 14 or 28 days as well as following in vitro exposure to 50 and 100 µM (Table 2). The weights of the subgroups were close to each other (12.4 %-12.75 %) (Table 2). Additional subgroup analysis taking into account the source of ChE (plasma, erythrocytes, and brain) or the type of statin used did not reveal a significant effect with pseudo-R2 values of only 0.23 % and 1.6 %, respectively.

sec.title: Funnel plot and the publication bias
sec.p: By examining the funnel plot (SE vs. effect size), the distribution of effect size points were not symmetrically distributed within the designated area of the plot (Fig. 4). This figure suggested some sort of publication bias. Furthermore, quantitative analysis by applying Egger’s regression test supported this observation, as it was statistically significant (t = 3.74, p < 0.0001). However, the trim-and-fill analysis which is complementary to the funnel plot did not reveal the need to add imputed points as an adjustment to the combined effect size (Fig. 4).

caption.p: Funnel plot to examine publication bias in studies used for the mini meta-analysis on plasma, erythrocyte and brain cholinesterase activities in experimental mice treated with statins.

sec.title: Risk of bias
sec.p: Fig. 5 depicts that the assessment of the risk of bias of studies included in the present meta-analysis was of a moderate (unclear) level. This is because the studies of the meta-analysis did not apply in ChE assays concealed allocation and blind intervention because of the unavailability of additional technical assistance during the experiments. To this end, the overall assessment of the risk of bias was judged to be “moderate”. In support of the low risk of bias, the total score of each study was high at 18 out of 20 (90 %), as the total score of 20 (100 %) indicates no risk of bias.

caption.p: Risk of bias distribution of studies A [14], B [16], C [17], and D [26] used for the mini meta-analysis on plasma, erythrocyte and brain cholinesterase activities in experimental mice treated with statins.

sec.title: Identification of the mouse protein targets for statins
sec.p: The main protein targets in the mouse body predicted in silico for the statins atorvastatin, simvastatin and rosuvastatin are shown in Table 3 and Fig. 6. The majority of protein target classes and their percentage ranges as predicted in silico by the Swiss TargetPrediction webserver are Family AG protein- coupled receptor (20.0 %-33.3 %), Oxidoreductase (6.7–13.3 %) and Eraser (13.3 % each). Additional protein targets for atorvastatin are nuclear receptors (26.7 %), enzyme (20.0 %) and phosphodiesterase (6.7 %); for simvastatin, they are electrochemical transporter (13.3 %) and 6.7 % of each of enzyme, kinase, ligase, protease, voltage-gated ion channel, family BG protein-coupled receptor and phosphatase. Those of rosuvastatin are electrochemical transporter, kinase and protease at 6.7 %, 20.0 % and 13.3 %, respectively. Specific protein targets such as HMG-CoA reductase-the specific statin target (probability= 0.953–1.0) within the Oxidoreductase class, dopamine transporter and norepinephrine transporter (probability= 0.959) within the electrochemical transporter class, and neurokinin 2 receptor (probability= 0.959) within the Family AG protein-coupled receptor class are also presented in Fig. 6.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The mini meta-analysis of the 72 ChE activity records revealed that statin treatments in mice significantly reduced the enzyme activity by 25.85 %, as the combined effect size of the forest plot was 74.15 %. This effect size was dependent on doses and concentrations of statins used in mice, as it was revealed by the subgroup analysis because of the high-level heterogeneity of the results. There are two types of ChE, the pseudo-ChE of the plasma (butyrylcholinesterase, EC 3.1.1.8) and true ChE of the brain and erythrocytes (acetylcholinesterase; EC 3.1.1.7) [44], [45], [46], [47], [48]. The present meta-analysis showed that pseudo- and true ChE activities were affected by the statins, a situation encountered with organophosphate and carbamate insecticides that variably inhibit both types of the enzyme [44], [45], [49]. However, caution should be exercised when assessing the extent of ChE inhibition due to inherent intra-individual, inter-individual, and baseline variations in ChE activity, which may also fluctuate over time [44], [49], [50], [51]. Within this context, the true ChE is mainly associated with neuronal cholinergic functions, especially when exposure occurs to drugs and toxicants [44], [45]. Furthermore, ChE activity in the plasma aside from its metabolic role [46] could act as a marker of low-grade or even severe systemic inflammations [47], [48]. The statin-induced changes in ChE activities as shown by the present meta-analysis further support the overall concept of the involvement of this enzymatic changes in the cholinergic modulation of various neurobehavioral functional aspects [13], [14], [16], [17] as well as learning and memory [9], [19], [23], [32] in laboratory animals.

Clinically, statins exhibit variable and differential effects on blood ChE activities [52], [53], [54], [55], [56]. For instance, long-term treatment of patients with coronary artery disease using atorvastatin and rosuvastatin has been reported to reduce butyrylcholinesterase and erythrocyte ChE activities that were initially elevated above normal values [53]. In contrast, lovastatin and simvastatin decreased butyrylcholinesterase activity, while mevastatin and pravastatin did not significantly affect the enzyme. Additionally, other studies have reported no observable effects of statins on blood ChE activities [54], [55], [56]. This variability indicates that the pharmacological impact of statins on ChE activities is not uniform across different statins and patient populations.

Given that ChE inhibitors delay the onset of Alzheimer's disease and slow clinical progression of the disease, statins may offer additional therapeutic benefits for patients with dementia [57], [58]. As statins are devoid of neurocognitive risks, they could be positioned as neuroprotective agents to prevent or delay the onset of dementia [59]. Clinical evidence supports this hypothesis by indicating a reduced dementia risk in statin-treated patients [60], suggesting potential repurposing of statins for pleiotropic effects beyond modulation of blood cholesterol levels [5], [8], [32], [59]. Moreover, statins exhibit differential inhibition of ChE activity [12], [52], [61], [62], [63]. Therefore, further investigations utilizing in vitro experimental models-specifically combining blood ChE with inhibitor incubation prior to enzyme activity measurement [26]-could clarify the potential anti-ChE actions of these drugs, as in vitro ChE inhibition by statins closely mirrors their in vivo effects [12], [14], [16], [17], [18], [19], [61].

The source of heterogeneity was found by the present subgroup analysis to be in vivo doses and in vitro concentrations of the three statins (Fig. 3, Table 2). Nevertheless, the data points appeared to be homogenous across the studies included as they did not deviate from normal distribution and were located within the limits of the regression analysis within the effect zone, with no outliers. Egger’s regression analysis and the related funnel showed significant publication bias. This could be due to limited studies in conjunction with selectivity in reporting the results [34], [35], [36], [37]. However, ChE records of studies included in the present meta-analysis were not selectively reported as they even included non-significant outcomes (Table 1). Further, the trim-and-fill analysis did not add imputed data points to the funnel plot, hence underscoring the overall publication bias. Nevertheless, additional analysis is needed when more statin-ChE data in mice become available. Assessing the risk of bias of studies subjected to the present meta-analysis indicated that it was of moderate level. This is because of the “moderate” answers given to sub-questions on concealed allocation and blind intervention since additional technical assistance could not be recruited during the experiments. However, the total score of each study was high enough (90 %, 18 out of 20) to lean towards the low bias level.

Numerous body proteins were predicted to be targets for the three statins (atorvastatin, simvastatin and rosuvastatin) by applying the Swiss TargetPrediction tool. Despite the differential protein targeting for these statins, the main ones included Family AG protein-coupled receptor, Oxidoreductase, Eraser, nuclear receptor, enzyme, phosphodiesterase, electrochemical transporter, kinase and ligase that varied from 6.7 % to 33.3 %. These target proteins are highly involved in the physiological functions of many body systems as well as in their pathological processes and disease conditions, and they are potential targets for medications and drug discovery [27], [28], [42], [43], [64], [65]. To name a few examples, the family AG protein-coupled receptors have been implicated in Alzheimer’s disease in association with interaction with ChE inhibitors and signal pathways to molecular-based therapeutic approach [59], [60], [63], [64], [65]. Oxidoreductases are large enzymatic entities with substrate diversity that catalyze oxidative reactions in the body and are involved in drug biotransformation and detoxification [66], [67]. Erasers have been associated with cellular metabolic processes such as ADP-ribose-dependent mechanisms [68], whereas phosphodiesterases hydrolyze cyclic nucleotides to modulate cellular metabolic events, and they are targets for many therapeutic manipulations that involve the cardiovascular system and autoimmunity [69], [70]. Within this context, it is reasonable to deduce that numerous metabolic pathways and drug-related pharmacodynamic processes are associated with these proteins.

The protein targets for statins reported in the present study, further signal their potential interrelationship with the cholinergic system [4], [14], [18], [60], [61], [62], [63], since statins reduce the ChE activity (Fig. 1), which is considered a new statin target other than the 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A [1], [2]. These target proteins additionally highlight their possible roles in the pleiotropic actions of statins as identified in disease conditions such as Alzheimer’s disease and cognitive functions [5], [8], [9], [19], [22], [23], [32], [59], [60]. They would also serve to be the basis for in-depth exploration of statin intolerance [10], [11], adverse effects [6], [7], [14], [15], [16], [17], [24] as well as statin-protein docking techniques [64], [65].

sec.title: Limitations
sec.p: The present meta-analysis is limited in scope to highlight statin effects on the ChE activity in the mouse. However, it was concise by involving 72 ChE records in the blood and the brain from recent publications [14], [16], [17], [26]. We only tested three statins (atorvastatin, simvastatin and rosuvastatin), therefore, additional explorations involving other statins are needed, since they differ in their pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties [1], [2], [3], [4]. We did not attempt to analyze possible statin-protein docking interaction, since it was out of the scope of the present study.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: The present mini meta-analysis highlights the experimental impact of statin treatments in mice by reducing blood and brain ChE activities, in a dose/concentration-dependent manner, that would potentially modulate the cholinergic system. This pattern could be robust at present; nevertheless, it needs additional in-depth exploration to examine other statins and various body systems. This anti-ChE effect together with the in silico recognized protein targets could be the basis of further explorations to understand statin intolerance, and expand prospects of their roles in pleiotropic actions and adverse effects.
